language_wrapper: Let {a} and {k} be fixed positive integers with {k} \ge 2. Define S to be the set of positive integers whose prime factorizations contain at least {k} prime factors, counted with multiplicity (for example, 12 = 2^2\cdot 3 lies in S when {k} \le 3). What is the largest positive integer that is not the sum of a positive integral multiple of {a} and an element of S?
hardness_rationale: The seed problem relies on covering residues modulo a fixed modulus with composite numbers and locating a tight threshold beyond which all integers are representable. Our family strengthens the additive restriction from "composite" (Ω(n) ≥ 2) to "having at least k prime factors counted with multiplicity" (Ω(n) ≥ k) for k ≥ 2. This sparser set complicates residue coverage and heightens the threshold that must be established via Chinese Remainder Theorem and modular inverses using carefully chosen moduli. The solver must construct minimal representatives in each residue class by forcing divisibility by a product of k primes coprime to a, then argue that all sufficiently large integers are representable using these fixed class witnesses. Finally, an exact maximum requires a nontrivial computational check below the threshold, made challenging by the multiplicity-based factor counting instead of simple compositeness. This layering of CRT, modular inverses, and distribution of k-almost-primes elevates the difficulty substantially beyond the seed.
notes:
Proof of correctness (sketch): Fix a and k ≥ 2. Choose distinct primes q1, ..., qk none dividing a, and set P = q1⋯qk. Then gcd(a, P) = 1. For each residue r modulo a, the system s ≡ r (mod a), s ≡ 0 (mod P) has a solution by the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Let s_r be the least positive solution for residue r. Since P | s_r, s_r has at least k prime factors (with multiplicity), so s_r ∈ S. For any N ≥ s_r + a with N ≡ r (mod a), we have m = (N − s_r)/a ≥ 1 integer and N = a·m + s_r with s_r ∈ S, hence N is representable. Therefore all N ≥ T := max_r(s_r) + a are representable, so the set of non-representable integers is finite and its maximum lies below T. The verifier computes s_r via modular inverse of a modulo P, builds a sieve to count Ω(n) efficiently, and searches for the exact largest non-representable below T. The construction of P guarantees residue coverage and thus finiteness of the complement. The difficulty constraints ensure instances are nontrivial and that brute force cannot short-circuit without the CRT threshold argument.
Implementation notes: The generator selects a in [36, 84] with at least two distinct prime factors and k ∈ {2, 3}. It ensures gcd(a, P) = 1 by choosing small primes among {3,5,7,11,13} not dividing a, and limits P to keep the threshold manageable. The verifier recomputes P deterministically from the smallest eligible primes, thereby remaining independent of generation and robust. The sieve-based Ω counting yields good performance up to moderate thresholds.
Generalization clarity: The family replaces "composite" with "Ω(n) ≥ k" for arbitrary k ≥ 2, preserving the core idea of residue class coverage while requiring a stronger modular construction and a more delicate finite search.
source_question: What is the largest positive integer that is not the sum of a positive integral multiple of 42 and a positive composite integer?
